paras: The Point Pleasant Christmas disturbance of 1880 was a day of drinking, street fighting and racial threats among crowds of white and Black men on Main Street in Point Pleasant, West Virginia, on December 25, 1880. Men on each side threatened to drive the other race from town and drew weapons, but no shot was fired and no one was arrested. The town's weekly paper called it a disgrace and urged arrests, the closing of saloons and, failing official action, a vigilance committee.

According to the Weekly Register, a number of "worthless whites and worthless negroes" began drinking early on Christmas morning, and by nine o'clock many were drunk, cursing and quarreling among themselves. They then began to insult and assault people passing along the streets, and officers who tried to enforce the law were resisted, cursed and threatened. Hundreds of people stayed on the streets all day, expecting a "bloody riot" at any moment.

Crowds of whites and Blacks gathered at several points on Main Street, where some men urged a fight and drew revolvers and knives while others tried to calm them. The paper reported that some Black men threatened "to clean out the whites and take the town," and some white men threatened "to clean out the negroes and drive them from the town." It attributed these threats to "the lower order of whites and blacks" and said other residents readied arms and ammunition in case of an outbreak, which did not come.

Not one participant of either race was arrested, although the Register held that at least twenty-five men should have been jailed. The paper asked the Mayor to arrest, try and fine those involved and the next Grand Jury to indict the ringleaders. No report of arrests, indictments or a vigilance committee appears in the later coverage found.

The only known account is the Point Pleasant Weekly Register of December 29, 1880, which treated the day as a local scandal under the heading "Local Matters" and in a one-line note that "Rowdyism" had been "rampant" on Christmas. The editor called the day "a disgrace to the town" and the officers' conduct "a burlesque upon law and order," and blamed men of both races equally, warning that a single shot would have brought on "a war of races."

The editorial blamed the saloons and urged voters to abolish them at the March town election. It went further, proposing that if officers would not act, a "Vigilance Committee" should make the "roughs and rowdies" of both races behave "or else to rid the town of them entirely," while admitting the editor was not "much of an advocate" of taking the law into private hands. No other newspaper's report of the episode appears in the coverage.

accounts.gist: Drunken men of both races filled Main Street, threatened each other's race and the town, and drew weapons; a race riot was expected all day but did not break out, and the officers arrested no one.
